To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the interaction of the polymerase-associated (PAD) domain of yeast Rev1 with proliferating cell nuclear (PCNA) antigen occurs at the non-canonical site on PCNA, near the interm monomer interface, and that the interaction is disrupted by a double amino acid mutation at the interface.

the non-canonical binding site of PCNA near the intermolecule interface is required for the interaction of yeast Rev1 with PCNA and that the interaction is specifically required for Polζ/Rev-dependent translesion DNA synthesis (TLS).
The non-canonical protein binding site at the monomer monomer interface of yeast PCNA regulates the interaction of PCNA and Rev1 and the Rev1-Polζ dependent translesion DNA synthesis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the regulation of DNA replication and the maintenance of genome integrity in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
the mechanism by which the PCNA protein regulates the access of DNA polymerases to the DNA replication fork.
the regulation of translesion synthesis in eukaryotes and the role of proliferating cell nuclear antigens (PCNA).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this work shows that the noncanonical protein-binding site at the monomer–monomer interface of yeast PCNA regulates the Rev1- and Polζ-dependent TLS pathway.
the non-canonical binding site of Rev1 at the intermolecular PCNA interface is required for the Rev1/PCNA/Polζ-dependent translesion DNA synthesis.
the non-canonical PCNA-binding site at the intermolecular PCNA interface is used by the Polζ-Rev1 complex in the TLS of damaged DNA.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the non-canonical PCNA-binding site at the monomer interface is required for the interaction of yeast PCNA with Rev1 and Pol ζ.
the noncanonical binding site at the monomer interface of PCNA is used for the interaction of Rev1 and Polz with PCNA.
the PCNA monomer-monomers interface is a novel protein-protein interaction site that is used by Rev1 and Polε to coordinate the TLS pathway with the DNA replication fork.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the interaction of PCNA at the monomer-monomer interface is not restricted to Polζ and Rev 1 but may represent a general feature of protein-protein interaction with the trimeric ring.
the non-canonical protein binding site at the intermolecular face of PCNA is used by the Rev1/PCNA complex to regulate the access of Rev1 to the primer termini of the replicating DNA.
yeast Polζ and Rev-1 use a novel binding site near PCNA intermolecular interface for their interaction with PCNA and that this site is required for Rev1/Pol ζ dependent TLS.
